title: Nocturne debrief — Amir Nadeem — Sr Runtime
content:
Context: informal late-night debrief after loop with Amir Nadeem for Senior Runtime Engineer. Panel: Evan (systems), Mikael (infra), me (serving runtime + oncall). 60m loop: 30m architecture + 30m coding/design exercise. Candidate came recommended by a contractor reference; resume shows deep LLM-serving experience at a mid-size infra startup.

Quick gut summary (one paragraph):
- Amir is thoughtful, pragmatic, and has a strong mental model for memory/KV cache tradeoffs in autoregressive serving. He communicates tradeoffs well and surfaced edge cases I hadn’t anticipated (multi-tenant cache eviction interactions). On the flip side, his latency-first heuristics lean toward optimistic engineering assumptions (rare failure modes under tail latency were underexplored). I’m tentatively positive but want another short follow-up focused on SRE scenarios and a brief on-call simulation.

Signals that stood out (strengths):
- Clear framing of cache coherency problems for prefix caching; used a concrete example with request patterns and showed how eviction jitter can amplify tail latency.
- Practical quantization experience: walked through a quantization-compatibility checklist (weights, layernorm sensitivity, calibration runs) and when to prefer per-channel vs per-tensor.
- Good debugging stories: reproduced a KV-cache corruption scenario in a prod-like setting and traced root cause to async checkpoint ordering.
- Communication: concise, gave a one-minute summary before diving into details — good for cross-team work.

Risk signals / open concerns:
- On-call readiness felt thin: limited examples of triaging rolling restarts and multi-region failover under load. Explained what to do conceptually but no concrete runbook actions or shell commands.
- Some assumptions about request homogeneity (same token length distribution) — our workload is wide variance; didn’t proactively propose instrumentation to detect skew.
- Two brief math errors in throughput back-of-envelope (not blocking, but suggests lower caution under pressure).

Behavioral notes (verbatim-ish snippets and shorthand):
- "If you can cache prefixes across models, you can trade inference cost for memory — but eviction coordination is the tricky bit" — then sketched coordinator with lease-style locks.
- Repeatedly asked for example distributions; likes to ground answers in numbers.
- When pressed on what he would do during a P99 spike: prioritized isolating hot prefixes, rate-limiting heavy clients, then graceful degradation via lightweight model variant. Focus on graceful fallback was good.

Technical deepcut (high value):
- Gave a small pseudocode sketch for a continuous-batching loop that avoids head-of-line blocking by splitting long sequences into windowed micro-batches. This was original and aligned with some of our internal experiments — worth filing as a design note to experiment quickly.
- Proposed a simple KV checksum/versioning scheme to detect async write reorder; low overhead and easy to adopt in testing.

Scorecard (1-5 scale; quick draft):
- Systems design / architecture: 4
- Low-level implementation (data structures, algorithms): 4
- Production/operational maturity (on-call, SRE): 3
- Communication & cross-team: 5
- Role-fit (runtime focus): 4

Suggested composite recommendation: "hire with a short operational probation". Rationale: strong alignment with runtime and model-serving problems, high communication value for team knowledge-sharing. Primary mitigation: require a 4-week on-call shadow and a targeted runbook-writing exercise focused on multi-region failover and tail-latency triage.

Concrete next steps (actionable):
1) Send this draft to panel for quick +/0/- votes (Evan, Mikael) and ask explicitly for any counterexamples to the runbook requirement.
2) If panel leans +, invite Amir to a 30m follow-up: on-call simulation (tabletop) + quick whiteboard on instrumentation for skew detection. Keep it focused and scheduled asap.
3) If moving forward, include in offer: a week of paid pairing and a defined 4-week ramp with specific SLO-oriented checkpoints (P95/P99 reduction ownership for first 6 weeks).

Suggested follow-up interview sketch (30m):
- 10m: SRE scenario walkthrough: rolling restart under rising P99, what metrics to check, what commands to run, abort criteria.
- 10m: Short code review / bug-fix exercise: read a small repro that leaks KV entries during rapid rotations, ask candidate to propose changes.
- 10m: Rapid-fire instrumentation plan: what metrics, tracing, and alert thresholds would you add in the first 48h?

Quick on-call rubric to include if hired (for probation):
- Week 0-1: shadowing + read-only access to runbooks
- Week 2: own small ops task (deploy a cache config change in staging)
- Week 3-4: rotate on-call under mentor; required to author or update one runbook for multi-region incidents
- Success criteria: can lead a P99 mitigation in staging and author a checklist that captures at least 6 actionable runbook steps.

Notes to self / meta thoughts (rough):
- Filing: move the micro-batching pseudocode to our internal drafts repo (tag: micro-batch-nocturne) — Evan will be interested.
- Watch for over-indexing on graceful fallback. We need someone who can balance graceful degradation with fast recovery; follow-up must press on concrete recovery actions.
- Candidate likely strong mentor for juniors given communication style — high multiplier.

Checklist before final panel note-out:
- [ ] Get Evan and Mikael votes + short sentence each
- [ ] Send follow-up invite template (I can draft)
- [ ] Draft offer skeleton contingent on runbook probation

End of scratchpad. This is intentionally informal — will polish into a panel-facing debrief once I have votes.
